stages.title: Needs and wants
stages.hook: You are hungry and you also want a new toy. Which one do you really need today?
explain: A need is something we must have to live. Food, water, a safe place to sleep and clothes are needs.
A want is something nice to have. A toy, a sweet or a game is a want. We can live without wants.
Money is often not enough for everything. So we think: needs first, then wants.

example.q: Ama has 5 coins. Bread costs 3 coins. A toy costs 4 coins. What should she buy first?
steps: Bread is food. Food is a need.
Buy the need first: bread, 3 coins.
She has 2 coins left. That is not enough for the toy.
example.a: The bread, because it is a need.

analogies.home: Dinner on the table is a need. A new picture book is a want.
analogies.farm: A farmer needs water for the plants. A bright new hat is only a want.
analogies.nature: A bird needs food and a nest. It does not need shiny things.
analogies.city: A bus ticket to school is a need. A fun balloon on the street is a want.

stages.mnemonic: Need = Never go without. Want = Would be nice.
terms: Something you must have to live.
Something nice to have but not a must.
To pick one thing instead of another.

misc.wrong: If I really want something, it is a need.
misc.right: A strong wish does not make something a need. Needs keep us alive and healthy.

stages.limits: People sometimes disagree about what is a need. A warm coat is a need in a cold place but less so in a hot place.

trip.prompt: Look for the things every person needs to live.

questions.q: Which one is a need?
questions.why: We must drink water to live. The others are wants.

questions.q: Which one is a want?
questions.why: We can live without a game, so it is a want.

questions.q: A need is something you...
questions.why: Needs are the things that keep us alive and well.

questions.q: Kofi is cold and it is raining. What does he need most?
o: A new red ball to play with
questions.why: Staying warm and dry keeps him well, so the coat is a need.

questions.q: Lina has only a few coins. She needs lunch and wants a comic. What is a wise choice?
questions.why: Needs come first. If coins are left, she can think about wants.

questions.q: Is a bicycle always a want?
o: No. It can be a need if it is the only way to get to school
Yes, because a bicycle is only ever for fun and games
No, because a bicycle is a kind of food
questions.why: What is a need can change with where and how we live.

questions.q: Match each thing to need or want.
pairs: A need, because it is food
A want, because it is for fun
A need, because we must drink
A treat we could live without
questions.why: Bread and water keep us alive. A toy and sweets are nice but not needed.

questions.q: Why do we think about needs first?
o: Because we need them to stay alive and well
Because wants cost much more than needs do
Because shops always sell them first of all
questions.why: Wants are not bad. Needs simply matter first for our health and safety.

questions.q: Ama has 10 coins. A meal (a need) costs 6 coins. How many coins are left for wants?
questions.why: 10 − 6 = 4 coins are left.

questions.q: Put these in order: what Ama should do first to last.
questions.why: Cover needs first, then see what is left for wants.

panel.q: Two children disagree: one says a phone is a need, the other says it is a want. What is the best response?
o: It can depend on the person and place, so give reasons
The first child is wrong and the second is right, so no reasons are needed
panel.why: Some things are needs for some people, for example to call for help. Good thinkers give reasons.

panel.q: Why is it hard to buy every want we have?
panel.model: We do not have enough money for everything, so we must choose, usually needs first.
panel.why: Money is limited, so we choose.

panel.q: A family has little money. Which choice shows careful thinking?
o: Pay for food and school things, then wants if any money is left
Buy toys and treats first, then food only if some money is left
Spend all the money on one big want
panel.why: Careful thinkers cover needs before wants.

teach.topic: The difference between a need and a want
teach.model: A need is something you must have to live, like food and water. A want is nice to have, like a toy. We think about needs first. For example, bread is a need but a toy is a want.

points.ask: Which one do we pick first?
Can you give me an example?

stages.title: Money and its uses
stages.hook: Long ago people had no coins. How did they get what they wanted? Why do we use money now?
explain: Money is what we use to pay for things. It can be coins, paper notes or a card.
Money helps us buy what we need. It also lets us keep value for later, when we save it.
Every country has its own money. A shop will give you things when you give the right amount of money.

example.q: Tariq gives the baker 5 coins for a loaf of bread. What is the money used for?
steps: The coins pay for the bread.
example.a: The money pays for the bread.

analogies.home: A jar of coins at home can pay for milk later.
analogies.city: At the market, coins turn into fruit.
analogies.farm: A farmer sells eggs and gets coins. Then the coins buy seeds.
analogies.tech: A card or phone can pay too, but it is still money.

stages.mnemonic: Money is a magic ticket: give it, get something.
terms: What we use to pay for things.
A small round piece of metal money.

misc.wrong: Money is only coins and notes.
misc.right: Money can also be digital, like numbers on a card or phone.

stages.limits: In the past people also used shells, salt and other things as money. What counts as money has changed over time.

trip.prompt: Find pictures of money from different times and places.

questions.q: What is money used for?
o: To wear it on your head
questions.why: We give money so we can get things.

questions.q: Which one is money?
questions.why: Coins are money. The others are not used to pay.

questions.q: Price means...
o: how many days it takes to get to you
questions.why: The price tells us how many coins to pay.

questions.q: Why is money useful when we save it?
o: It grows by itself in a pocket
questions.why: Saved money keeps its value so we can buy things later.

questions.q: Mina sells apples and gets coins. What can she do with the coins?
o: Nothing at all, coins are useless
Plant them in the garden to grow more
questions.why: Money from selling can buy other things.

questions.q: A pear costs 2 coins. Ben buys 3 pears. How many coins does he pay?
questions.why: 3 × 2 = 6 coins.

questions.q: Ana has 10 coins. She buys a book for 7 coins. How many coins are left?
Why is it easier to use money than to swap goods?
o: Everyone can accept money for anything
Money is heavy and hard to carry about
Money is a kind of food
Money is free and anyone can take it
questions.why: With swapping, both people must want what the other has. Money works for every trade.

questions.q: Match the word to its meaning.
pairs: A round piece of metal money
questions.why: These are the basic money words.

questions.q: A shop in a new country does not take your coins. What is the likely reason?
o: Each country uses its own money
Shops in new places hate coins
Coins are too small to be seen there
questions.why: Countries have different kinds of money.

panel.q: Why might shells or salt have been used as money long ago?
o: People agreed they were worth something and could swap them
They were handed out free by the town each morning
panel.why: Money works when people trust it and accept it.

panel.q: Why do we trust a coin to buy bread when a plain stone cannot?
panel.model: Everyone agrees that coins are worth something, but a stone is not accepted as payment.
panel.why: Money works because people accept it.

panel.q: Why do we keep some money for later?
o: We may need things we cannot yet predict
Money goes bad if you hold it for too long
Shops close for ever each year
Coins fall apart after a day
panel.why: Saving helps with future needs.

teach.model: Money is what we use to pay for things like bread. A price tells how much money something costs. We can also save money to use later. For example, I give coins and I get a toy.

points.ask: What do we do with money?
Can we keep it for later?
Can you give me an example?

stages.title: Buying and selling
stages.hook: At a market, one person gives food and the other gives coins. Who is the buyer and who is the seller?
explain: A buyer gives money to get something. A seller gives something and gets money.
The price is the number of coins the seller asks. The buyer can say yes or no.
A shop sells things. People buy them. Both can be happy with a fair deal.

example.q: A seller sells 4 mangoes at 2 coins each. How many coins does the buyer pay?

analogies.farm: A farmer sells milk. A family buys it.
analogies.city: A baker sells bread. A student buys it.
analogies.sea: A fisher sells fish at the harbour.
analogies.sport: At a match, a seller offers drinks and fans buy them.

terms: A person who pays to get something.
A person who gives something and gets paid.
Money given back when you pay too much.

misc.wrong: Only the seller gains from a sale.
misc.right: Both can gain. The buyer gets something useful and the seller gets money.

stages.limits: Sometimes prices are not fair, or people feel pushed to buy. Careful shoppers compare before they buy.

trip.prompt: Look at pictures of markets. Who are the buyers and sellers?

questions.q: Who pays money in a sale?
questions.why: The buyer pays and the seller is paid.

questions.q: Who gets the money?
questions.why: The seller gets money for what is sold.

questions.q: Sita gives 3 coins for a banana. Sita is the...
questions.why: She pays, so she is the buyer.

questions.q: What is change?
o: Money given back when you pay too much
A new shop that opens up in the town
The price written on a label
A coin that you have lost on the road
questions.why: If you pay more than the price, the seller gives change.

questions.q: Each toy costs 3 coins. Leo buys 2 toys. How many coins does he pay?
Zara pays 10 coins for a snack that costs 7 coins. How many coins of change does she get?
A seller asks 5 coins for a hat. You think it is too much. What can you do?
o: Say no or look in another shop
You must buy it, no matter what
Cry until the seller gives it away
questions.why: Buyers can choose not to buy at that price.

questions.q: Match each person to what they do.
questions.why: These are the parts of a sale.

questions.q: Why can a sale be good for both people?
o: The buyer gets what they want and the seller gets money
Only the buyer gains, because they take the thing home
questions.why: Each person gets something they value more than what they give.

questions.q: Put the sale in order.
questions.why: First choose, then learn the price, then pay, then take the item.

panel.q: A seller has many apples that no one wants to buy. What might the seller do?
panel.why: A lower price may bring buyers, though the seller must still cover costs.

panel.q: Why should a buyer ask the price before paying?
panel.model: The buyer needs to know the cost, to see whether they have enough money and decide if it is fair.
panel.why: Knowing the price helps us decide.

panel.q: Two shops sell the same bread. One costs 3 coins, one costs 4. What is a careful choice?
o: Compare and buy the cheaper one if quality is the same
Always buy the dearer one because it must be better
panel.why: Comparing helps save money when other things are equal.

teach.model: A buyer pays money to get something. A seller gives the thing and gets the money. The price says how much to pay. For example, I pay 2 coins to the baker and get bread.

points.ask: How do we know how much to pay?
Can you show me an example?

stages.title: Saving money
stages.hook: You get 5 coins today. If you spend all of them, what will you have tomorrow?
explain: Saving means keeping some money and not spending it now.
We save for something big, or for a day when we need money.
A piggy bank, a jar or a bank can keep savings safe. Saving a little each week adds up.

example.q: Omar saves 2 coins each week. How many coins does he have after 4 weeks?

analogies.home: A jar on a shelf holds coins for later.
analogies.nature: A squirrel keeps nuts for winter. That is like saving.
analogies.farm: A farmer keeps some grain to plant next year.
analogies.tech: A phone wallet can show how much you have saved.

stages.mnemonic: Save a little, grow a lot: drop a coin in the pot.
terms: Keep money for later instead of spending it.
A safe place that keeps money.

misc.right: Saving means spending wisely and keeping some for later.

stages.limits: Some families cannot save much because they must spend on needs first. Saving is hard when money is short.

trip.prompt: Find ways people keep savings safe.

questions.q: What does it mean to save money?
questions.why: Saving is keeping money to use later.

questions.q: Where can money be kept safe?
o: A bank or a piggy bank
questions.why: Banks and piggy banks are safer places.

questions.q: Why might Nia save her coins?
o: To hide from friends and not play
To make the coins grow smaller
questions.why: Saving helps us reach a goal.

questions.q: Pia saves 3 coins each week. How many coins does she have after 3 weeks?
A toy costs 12 coins. Sam has saved 7 coins. How many more coins does he need?
Which is saving?
o: Putting 2 of your 5 coins in a jar
Spending all 5 coins on sweets now
questions.why: Saving means keeping some money.

questions.q: A squirrel stores nuts for winter. How is this like saving?
o: It eats every nut right now
It gives all the nuts away
It forgets where the nuts are
questions.why: Both keep something for a later time.

questions.q: The roof leaks and the family needs coins quickly. How does saving help?
o: There is money ready for the problem
The roof mends itself if you wait long enough
Saving makes the rain stop falling
questions.why: Savings can pay for surprises.

questions.q: Match the words.
questions.why: These are the saving words.

questions.q: Which plan helps you reach a 20-coin goal?
o: Put a few coins away each week
Spend all your coins at once and hope for more
Wait for new coins to just appear
questions.why: Small steady savings add up.

panel.q: Some people cannot save much. Which is the best explanation?
o: Needs may use up all their money
They do not like coins and so give them away
panel.why: When needs cost almost all income, there is little to save. It is not about character.

panel.q: Why is it good to have a goal when you save?
panel.model: A goal tells you what you are saving for and how much you need, so you keep going until you reach it.
panel.why: A goal gives saving a purpose.

panel.q: If you spend now and save nothing, what is a possible problem?
o: You will have too much money
panel.why: Spending everything leaves no money for later.

teach.model: Saving means keeping some money for later instead of spending it all. We save for a goal or for a day when we need money. For example, I put coins in a jar to buy a bicycle.

stages.title: Goods and services
stages.hook: A baker makes a loaf. A barber cuts hair. One you can hold. Which one?
explain: Goods are things you can touch, like bread, shoes and books.
Services are jobs people do for you, like cutting hair, driving a bus or teaching.
We buy both. Goods are made. Services are done.

example.q: Is a haircut a good or a service?
steps: Can you hold a haircut in your hand? No.
It is something a person does for you.

analogies.city: A bus ride is a service. The bus ticket you hold is a paper good.
analogies.farm: Eggs are goods. A vet who helps a sick cow gives a service.
analogies.sport: A football is a good. A coach who trains you gives a service.
analogies.home: A chair is a good. A plumber who fixes a tap gives a service.

stages.mnemonic: Goods you hold. Services are done for you.
terms: A thing you can touch and buy.
A person who makes goods or gives services.

misc.wrong: Only things you can hold are worth paying for.
misc.right: Services such as teaching, healing or driving are worth paying for too.

stages.limits: Some things mix both, like a restaurant meal that is food (a good) and being served (a service).

trip.prompt: Find examples of goods and services.

questions.q: Which is a good?
questions.why: Shoes are things you can touch.

questions.q: Which is a service?
o: A loaf of warm bread from the baker
questions.why: A doctor does work for you.

questions.q: A teacher teaches. This is a...
questions.why: Teaching is work done for others.

questions.q: A farmer grows rice. Rice is a...
questions.why: Rice is a thing you can touch.

questions.q: Match each to good or service.
pairs: A trip someone drives for you
Work a barber does for you
questions.why: Goods are things. Services are work done for you.

questions.q: Who gives a service?
questions.why: A driver does work to carry people.

questions.q: A cook sells you a hot meal. Why is it both a good and a service?
o: You get food, and the cook does work for you
Food is not a good, and the cook does no work for you
It has no price and is free
questions.why: Some things mix a thing and work.

questions.q: A haircut costs 4 coins and a comb costs 2 coins. How much for both?
Can a service be stored in a box for later?
o: No, it happens when the work is done
Yes, you can keep it in a box until you want it
questions.why: A service is an action, not a thing.

questions.q: A toy shop sells toys. A repair person fixes your bike. Which is the service?
questions.why: Fixing is work done for you.

panel.q: A video lesson online is not something you can touch. Is it a good or a service?
o: Usually a service, since someone does teaching work
A good, since you can keep it in a bag
panel.why: Digital things can be hard to classify, but a lesson is mostly teaching work.

panel.q: Why do towns need people who give services as well as people who make goods?
panel.model: People need things such as food and also help such as healing and teaching, so towns need both.
panel.why: Both meet needs.

panel.q: A repair shop fixes a broken radio. Which is the service?
panel.why: The fixing is the work done for you.

teach.model: Goods are things you can touch, like bread and shoes. Services are jobs people do for you, like cutting hair. We buy both. For example, a ball is a good and a coach is a service.

stages.title: Jobs and earnings
stages.hook: Where do grown-ups get money from? What do they do all day?
explain: A job is work that a person does, and they are paid for it. The money they get is called earnings or pay.
Farmers, nurses, drivers, builders and teachers all have jobs. Each job helps other people.
People use their earnings to pay for needs and wants. Some earn more per hour, some less, depending on the work and where they live.

example.q: Kim earns 3 coins for each hour. She works 4 hours. How much does she earn?

analogies.farm: A farmer is paid when the crop is sold.
analogies.city: A bus driver is paid for carrying people.
analogies.sea: A fisher is paid for fish caught and sold.
analogies.home: A parent who works earns money for the family's food.

terms: Work that you are paid for.
A person who does a job.

misc.wrong: Only jobs where you are paid are real work.
misc.right: Caring for family at home is real, valuable work even if it is unpaid.

stages.limits: Pay is not always fair. People with similar skills can be paid differently, and people argue about why.

trip.prompt: Look for jobs from different countries and what they do.

questions.q: What is a job?
o: Work that you are paid for
A kind of toy that you can play with
questions.why: A job is work for pay.

questions.q: Money you get for work is called...
questions.why: Earnings are what a worker gets paid.

questions.q: Which person has a job helping sick people?
questions.why: A nurse cares for people who are sick.

questions.q: Tom earns 5 coins an hour. He works 3 hours. How many coins does he earn?
Rosa earned 20 coins and spent 8 coins on food. How many coins are left?
Why do people go to work?
o: To earn money for what they need
Because coins drop from the sky each day
questions.why: Pay buys the needs of the family.

questions.q: Match the worker to what they do.
questions.why: Each job helps other people.

questions.q: Why does a town need many different jobs?
o: People need many different things done
Everyone wants to do the same job in town
questions.why: No one can do everything alone, so different jobs help each other.

questions.q: Is helping at home a kind of work?
o: Yes, even when nobody pays money
No, only paid work counts as work
Yes, but only grown-ups can do it
questions.why: Unpaid work such as caring and cooking is still useful.

questions.q: Put this in order.
questions.why: Work comes first, then pay, then spending and saving.

panel.q: Two workers do the same job in two different countries and get different pay. Which is a good thought?
o: Prices and living costs may differ, so we must look closer
The worker in the poorer country must be cheating the boss
Pay is always the same everywhere
panel.why: Pay and prices differ across places, so we compare carefully.

panel.q: Why does a baker need a farmer, and a farmer need a baker?
panel.model: The baker needs grain from the farmer, and the farmer buys bread, so each earns money from the other's work.
panel.why: Jobs depend on one another.

panel.q: Why might someone learn a new skill?
o: It may help them find a job or earn more
It makes your coins vanish when you use it
It stops all work for ever
panel.why: Skills can lead to jobs, though no skill guarantees pay.

teach.model: A job is work that you are paid for. The money you get is your earnings. People use earnings to pay for what they need. For example, a farmer grows food, sells it and earns coins.

points.ask: What do people get for work?
What do they do with it?

stages.title: Scarcity and choice
stages.hook: There is one cake and four hungry friends. What can they do?
explain: Scarcity means there is not enough of something for everyone to have all they want.
Because of scarcity, we must choose. If we pick one thing, we give up another.
What you give up is called the cost of your choice. Thinking about it helps us choose wisely.

example.q: Jo has 5 coins. A kite costs 5 coins and a ball costs 5 coins. What happens if Jo buys the kite?
steps: So Jo cannot buy the ball.
example.a: Jo gets the kite but gives up the ball.

analogies.home: One last cookie: if you eat it, your sister cannot.
analogies.farm: A field can grow maize or beans this year, not both in the same spot.
analogies.sport: A team can pick only some players for the match.
analogies.city: A city has money for a new park or a new road, but maybe not both.

stages.mnemonic: Scarce means not enough, so choose and let go.
terms: Not enough for everyone to have all they want.
Picking one thing instead of another.

misc.wrong: Scarcity only happens to poor people.
misc.right: Everyone faces scarcity, because time and money are limited for all.

stages.limits: People may choose differently and both can be sensible, because they value things differently.

trip.prompt: Find an example of something that is scarce.

questions.q: Scarcity means...
o: there is not enough for everyone to have all they want
there is far too much of everything to ever use up
questions.why: Scarce things are limited.

questions.q: If you buy a kite with all your coins, what happens?
o: You cannot buy something else with those coins
You get more coins to buy other things as well
The coins come back to you
questions.why: You give up other choices.

questions.q: There are 2 slices of cake and 3 children. This is...
questions.why: There is not enough for each to have one.

questions.q: Mina has time for TV or for a bike ride, not both. This shows...
questions.why: Time is limited so she must choose.

questions.q: You have 10 coins. A hat costs 6 coins. How many coins are left to spend on something else?
A cake is cut into 8 equal slices. 4 friends share it equally. How many slices does each get?
Does a rich person also face scarcity?
o: Yes, time and some things are still limited
No, because having lots of money fixes every limit
questions.why: Everyone has limited time, and some things cannot be bought.

questions.q: Match the idea to its meaning.
questions.why: These words fit together.

questions.q: A town has coins for a school or a pool. Which is a fair way to choose?
o: Talk about what people need most and why
Flip a coin and never think about it again
questions.why: Fair choices think about needs and listen to people.

questions.q: Why does thinking about what we give up help us?
o: It helps us pick the better choice
It stops scarcity from ever happening
questions.why: Knowing the cost of a choice helps us decide wisely.

panel.q: Can scarcity ever be fully removed?
o: Unlikely, because people can always want more than exists
Yes, if everyone agrees to stop wanting things for good
Yes, by just saying it is gone
Yes, if we count coins faster
panel.why: Wants are very large and resources are limited, so choices remain.

panel.q: Two friends want the last toy. Give one fair way to decide.
panel.model: They can take turns, share, or talk and agree on a fair way such as drawing lots.
panel.why: Fair ways let both feel respected.

panel.q: A family can pay for a trip or a new bed. Which statement is wisest?
o: It depends on their needs; talk and decide together
The trip is always the better choice, so just book it
panel.why: Different families value things differently. Good choices weigh needs.

teach.model: Scarcity means there is not enough for everyone to have all they want. So we must choose. When we pick one thing, we give up another. For example, with 5 coins I can buy a kite or a ball, not both.

points.ask: What happens to the other thing?

stages.title: Sharing and exchanging
stages.hook: You have an apple. Your friend has an orange. Can you both end up with something you like more?
explain: Sharing means letting others use or have some of what you have.
Exchanging, or swapping, means giving something to get something else. Long ago people mostly swapped. This is called barter.
A swap is good when both people feel they got something they like more than what they gave.

example.q: Ali has 2 bananas. Bea has 2 pears. They swap 1 for 1. What does each have?
steps: Ali gives 1 banana and gets 1 pear.
Bea gives 1 pear and gets 1 banana.
Each now has 1 banana and 1 pear.

analogies.home: Siblings share the toy box and swap stickers.
analogies.farm: A rice farmer swaps with a fisher: rice for fish.
analogies.sea: Two boats swap salt and fish at the dock.
analogies.sport: Cards are swapped between fans to finish a set.

stages.mnemonic: Give one, get one, both have fun.
terms: Let others use or have some of yours.
Give something to get something else.
Treating everyone with respect and equally.

misc.wrong: A swap only helps one person.
misc.right: In a willing swap, both people can feel better off.

stages.limits: Barter can be hard because each person must want what the other has. That is one reason money is useful.

trip.prompt: Find a place or time where people used barter.

questions.q: What is barter?
o: Buying things in a shop with coins
questions.why: Barter is swapping goods for goods.

questions.q: Sharing means...
o: keeping it all for yourself alone
questions.why: Sharing gives others a part.

questions.q: Kaya has extra rice. Ben has extra fish. They swap. Why is this good?
o: Rice is better than fish, so Ben loses
questions.why: A willing swap lets each gain what they like more.

questions.q: What makes a swap fair?
o: Both agree and feel it is a good deal
One person makes the other agree, even if it hurts
questions.why: Fair swaps are agreed freely.

questions.q: One hen is swapped for 6 eggs. How many eggs for 2 hens at the same rate?
A basket has 9 mangoes. 3 friends share them equally. How many does each get?
Mo wants beans, but the bean seller does not want his fish. What is the problem?
o: Barter needs both people to want what the other has
Beans cost nothing, so nobody needs to swap at all
questions.why: Barter needs a match of wants. Money solves that.

questions.q: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.why: These are ways people give and get.

questions.q: How does money help swaps?
o: It can be used to buy from anyone
It makes goods go bad faster when carried
It is very heavy to carry
questions.why: Money is accepted by everyone, so no matching of wants is needed.

questions.q: Put a fair swap in order.
questions.why: Agree first, then swap.

panel.q: Is it always better to share everything?
o: Sharing is kind, but people also need to keep what they need
Yes, always give away every single thing you own
panel.why: Sharing is good, yet people must also care for their own needs.

panel.q: Why can a swap make both people happier?
panel.model: Each person values what they get more than what they give, so both gain.
panel.why: People value things differently.

panel.q: A village with lots of fish and a village with lots of grain swap. What good thing happens?
o: Both villages have more kinds of food
One village ends up with less food than before
panel.why: Trade gives both more choice.

teach.model: Sharing means letting others have some of what you have. Swapping, or barter, means giving one thing to get another. A swap is good when both agree and both are happy. For example, I swap my apple for your orange.

stages.title: Simple personal budgeting
stages.hook: You get 10 coins each week. How can you plan so you do not run out before the week ends?
explain: A budget is a plan for your money. It says how much comes in and how much goes out.
A simple budget has three parts: needs, wants and savings. Needs come first.
Write down the plan, then check it at the end of the week. If money is left, it can go to savings.

example.q: Dara has 10 coins. She plans 5 for needs, 3 for wants and the rest for savings. How many coins does she save?

analogies.home: A family writes a list: food first, then fun, then a little for the jar.
analogies.farm: A farmer keeps some grain for food, some to sell and some for seeds.
analogies.city: A bus pass is bought first; then a snack if coins remain.
analogies.tech: A phone app can show where your coins went.

terms: A plan for how to use money.

misc.wrong: A budget is a rule that stops all fun.
misc.right: A budget is a plan that helps you pay for needs, enjoy some wants and save.

stages.limits: A budget is a plan, and surprises happen. Plans may need to change when prices or needs change.

trip.prompt: Look at how a simple budget is laid out.

questions.q: A budget is...
o: a special coin you keep in a box
questions.why: A budget plans how money is used.

questions.q: Money that comes in is called...
questions.why: Income is money received.

questions.q: In a simple budget, what should be paid first?
questions.why: Needs come before wants.

questions.q: You get 12 coins. You plan 6 for needs, 4 for wants. How many coins are left to save?
Kito saves 2 coins a week. How many coins after 5 weeks?
Lia has 15 coins. She spends 9. How many are left?
Sam spent all his coins on Monday and needs lunch on Friday. What went wrong?
o: He did not plan for the whole week
He saved too many coins on Monday and had none for fun
questions.why: A budget spreads money across the week.

questions.q: Why check your budget at the end of the week?
o: To see what worked and what to change
To lose some coins and start over again
Because shops ask to see it
questions.why: Checking helps us learn and plan better.

questions.q: Match the part of a budget.
questions.why: A budget shows all three.

questions.q: Put these budget steps in order.
questions.why: Know your money, plan, follow it, then review.

panel.q: Prices rise in the middle of the week. What is a sensible response?
o: Change the plan and keep needs first
Ignore the new price and keep the old plan exactly
panel.why: Budgets can be adjusted. Needs still come first.

panel.q: Why is a budget useful even if you have only a few coins?
panel.model: With few coins every coin matters, so a plan helps pay for needs and avoids running out.
panel.why: Planning matters most when money is tight.

panel.q: Two children plan differently: one saves more, one spends more on fun. Which statement is fair?
o: Both can be sensible if needs are covered
Only the saver is right, and the spender is not
panel.why: People value things differently. A good plan still covers needs.

teach.model: A budget is a plan for your money. It shows what comes in and what you spend. You pay for needs first, then wants, and put some aside to save. For example, with 10 coins I plan 5 for food, 3 for fun and 2 for the jar.

points.ask: Can you show me an example?
